utterances.text: The Podravanje was in the AOR of the Milici Brigade. As for how much Podravanje territory was within or out of the enclave is something that I really couldn't tell you. I can speak competently about the facilities and features in the AOR of my brigade, but I wouldn't go beyond that. I assume that the Podravanje Sector was outside of the demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I quite understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D145 now, please, thank you, which also relates to the intelligence data that was available to our units around the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Intelligence and Security Sector, of the 24th of June, 1995. The document talks about the activities from Srebrenica. And in the first paragraph, it states -- actually, the document is signed by myself, "Tolimir, Zdravko." We will see that on the second page later. The document states: "We hereby submit the following information on the enemy's intentions:" And the document is given to the commander of the 65th Motorised Regiment and the commander of the 67th PV, which is outside of the Main Staff. It states: "On 23rd of June of this year, at 0200 hours, a unit of approximately 300 soldiers headed out from Srebrenica, led by Ibrahim Mandzic, the commander of the 280th Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade; Vejiz Sabic, the commander of the 284th IBLB; his deputy, Semso Salihovic; and a guide, a man called Zoran Cardakovic. The unit's task was to insert itself on that same day at approximately 2000 hours into the general sector of Ruzina Voda, Han Pijesak municipality, via Zepa and Radava." Tell us, please, based on this first paragraph, are you able to tell us if you had heard of this Mandzic, Ibrahim and his unit that he led into Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of Ibrahim Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get this information about the activities of Mandzic's and Sabic's units, i.e., the 28th and the 284th's Light Brigades from Srebrenica in the direction of Han Pijesak, as it is stated in this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this information specifically. I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "In the above sector, this group is to use combat to attract the VRS forces in order to secure safe passage for Naser Oric, who is also travelling with a large group from the direction of Kladanj ..." Does this confirm, in part, the information that you provided about Naser Oric being in Tuzla and that he was supposed to break through from the direction of Tuzla, with a certain number of forces, to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, all I can do is confirm that we did have that information, the information as to the location of Naser Oric. And I can speak about what I wrote about the intentions of Naser Oric. As for the content of this information, that is something that I did not see, the one you are referring to right now. But you could connect that with the information that I had at my disposal and that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. In that case, we will not speak on this document anymore. Thank you. Can we now look at another document, which states -- actually, that is D52, and it's a B&H army document of the 8th of July, 1995. Its title is "Information About the Combat Results of the Units and Commands of the 28th Ground Army Division of the 2nd Corps of the B&H Army." Thank you. We can see in the second paragraph -- we don't have to read the whole document. This is a document written by those in charge of raising the morale of their troops, and the document states, actually in the first paragraph, about how they carried out actions from Zepa and Srebrenica against the Army of Republika Srpska and about their successes. And then it states : "Sixty Chetniks were liquidated, and according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." Then they talk about what was seized. And then in the third paragraph they speak about how large quantities of ammunition were seized in the village of Visnjica, and what the soldiers could not bring out, they destroyed by burning, as they say, as well as all the facilities that the aggressor could have used for military purposes. Can you please tell us whether you received the information about the village of Visnjica and how it was burned? Was this some information that was sent to the staff in the Han Pijesak, and does this confirm their actions in relation to Serbian units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now that I received any specific information relating to the village of Visnjica and what was going on there. That is the zone of responsibility of the Milici Brigade. However, in that period, I certainly did hear that there was an attack by the forces of the 28th Division from the enclave, directed at the village of Visnjica, which is in the municipality of Milici and, therefore, in the zone of responsibility of the Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at D67. This is also a document coming from the Intelligence Administration, Counter-Intelligence Department [as interpreted], of the BiH army. The date is the 13th of July, 1995, and it was forwarded through the commander of the 1st Corps to the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And here they inform Alija Izetbegovic what they did in relation to the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. You take a look at the document while we listen to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a correction for the record, so we have the description clear. This document purports to emanate from the Counter-Electronic Warfare Unit, not the Counter-Intelligence Unit, just so that there's no confusion in the record about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer, for this correction. This was, indeed, the Counter-Electronic Warfare Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If we look at the first paragraph, we see: "In view of the situation of our enclaves during the preceding period, the Army General Staff has undertaken a series of military activities and procedures to organise the members of the army in the enclaves and prepare them for possible developments, primarily the defence of the existing free territory and planned engagement and preparations for future joint operations and planned operations. "Specifically, the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa: "To start with, lethal assets and MTS were brought in on foot in fairly small quantities; "Seventeen helicopter flights were carried out, in each of which a helicopter was hit." Then the third bullet point: "We managed to transport a number of heavily-wounded soldiers in a similar manner." And then the last bullet point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you move the first page in Serbian, please, move upwards for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And it says: "The Crni Labudovi unit was frequently mentioned as a unit which could accomplish operational and strategic moves. This is incorrect. They are good lads and a good brave and bold unit which successfully accomplishes its tasks." My question is: Were you aware that the Muslims' enclaves, Zepa and Srebrenica, and their army inside Zepa and Srebrenica, which was supposed to be a demilitarised zone, was being reinforced and supplied with weapons through helicopter flights, as we can see from this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware that the 28th Division was getting weapons from Tuzla and from Kladanj, and I knew that they had communication between Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and that they were bringing in certain materiel from Zepa. I also knew that in the area of Zepa, more precisely at Malo and Velika Polje, helicopters were landing, and I knew that that's where they were receiving people from Srebrenica and bringing in certain things, including weapons. Furthermore, I know for sure that in this general area -- I don't want to be more specific about the spot because I'm going to make a mistake, but I knew that for a certain period of time in that area we had one or two crews from my brigade. They were in charge of following and targeting those helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see now the table on the right-hand side in the English translation, and you can see how many of which calibres entered Zepa and Srebrenica, and you can also see the totals. Can we also see all the remaining lines in the table and the remaining pages so that we could see the signature of Rasim Delic at the bottom of this document. Thank you. So here we can see the signature of Army General Rasim Delic. Can we now take a look at 1D705. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You will tell us whether you recognise the contents of this document. It was dated on the 14th of March, 1995. The title is: "Enemy Units in the Area of Srebrenica." It goes on as follows: "During July of the previous year, a group of officers from the Main Staff spent some time in Sarajevo. It was organised by the UN. When they returned, they brought the information and instructions by the Main Staff of the BiH Army. The commander of this operative group is Naser Oric from Srebrenica, and his deputy is Avdo Palic from Zepa ." Based on this, my question is: After the armed forces in Zepa and Srebrenica grew, having received weapons and materiel, was it then necessary to reorganise those forces from the level of operative group to the level of division? You are a soldier and you know that a division is a higher level. Can you tell us anything more about this document and what you know about it? This document contains the list of the relevant units. Thank you. Or, rather, maybe you should first answer my first question: This reinforcement with weapons, did it cause the reorganisation of the Muslim army so that it was reorganised into a division, and it used to be an operative group? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what I knew at the time. I can only speak about the information I had at the time. In Srebrenica, for a long time there was between 15-, 16-, to 20.000 men fit for military service. Don't take this number as a constant. It varied through time. It wasn't the same all the time. I also knew that there was not -- there were not sufficient quantities of weapons in Srebrenica of any kind. It wasn't possible to arm all those individuals who were able-bodied and who were supposed to be engaged as soldiers. The supply of weapons through various channels, by helicopters and by other routes, I suppose that it created the need to reorganise that army and the need to form the division and the operations group. I can affirm only in this context that bearing in mind the estimates about the number of able-bodied men and bearing in mind what Srebrenica was and what status it had, my estimate was that it was necessary to reorganise that army into a higher level of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Could you take a look at the third paragraph now, the one containing the names of the brigades, 280th, 281st, 282nd, 283rd, and 284th East Bosnian Brigade. My question is: Were those brigades present in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica? Thank you. As far as you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in my assessments and almost all information that I sent up, I think that I spoke about precisely those brigades, 280th to 284th, and there was, I think, a mountain battalion and maybe some other units. I don't remember right now. But I can confirm that those units, those brigades, are the brigades about which I informed the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, take a look at what it says further on. Under "280th Light Infantry Brigade," it says: "The commander of the 280th Light Infantry Brigade is Ibrahim Handzic, aka Mrki." Or -- well, now I can't read what it says here. "Krki" or "Mandza." Or maybe "Mrki" or "Mandza." And his deputy is Ibrahim Sabovic, aka Siptar. Have you ever heard of those people? And as far as you know, did those people really perform certain functions in those brigades?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I can help about the interpretation. Here it says "Handzic," while the surname is "Mandzic." It was Ibrahim Mandzic. And his nicknames were "Mrki" or "Mandza." Excuse me. I know this Ibrahim Mandzic personally, or, rather, I knew him before the war and I saw him after the war. I know all the Mandzics who lived in the area of Potocari. At the time, I knew that this Mandzic was one of the commanders in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Take a look now at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should let the witness answer your question in full. You asked for the second person, and I think for your benefit it's better to wait for his answer. Can you tell us something about the other person, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thought that the witness was finished with his answers. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go on, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You also asked me about this other person, Ibrahim Sabovic. I don't know who he is, and I don't know this nickname, Siptar. So in short, I don't know the name, the surname, and I don't know the nickname. Maybe I know this person, but I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us take a look at the second page, if your answer is finished. I would like you to take a look at the names of the commanders that are listed always immediately after the number of the brigade. First we have the commander of the 281st Light East Bosnian Infantry Brigade. First, Zulfo Tursunovic; then Ibro Dudic, he's in the 282nd; then in the 283rd, Salihovic, Huso; and 284th, Vejiz Sabic. Did you hear anything about those commanders? Did you have any intelligence information about them, information that you received and then forwarded for the operations analysis in the command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm, for instance, Zulfo Tursunovic; I also knew him personally, before the war, I knew all his family, and I know that he was the commander of a brigade. Then I also already mentioned Ibrahim Mandzic; yes, I know that he was a commander in Potocari, and I also know him personally. Then I also know personally Vejiz Sabic. It says here that he hails from Konjevic Polje, which means Bratunac municipality. Now, as for Huso Salihovic, I don't know who that is. And I also do not know Ibro Dudic. But I was aware of the 282nd and the 283rd Brigade. It was also my assessment that that those brigades existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let us take a look at the last page, where we see the entire Srebrenica structure and also the names. We see the civilian structure in Srebrenica or the civilian government. And can you just take a look and tell us whether you knew these individuals and whether they were, indeed, in the functions as mentioned here next to their names? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the names that appear here look familiar and I can recognise them, but I have to tell you that I don't know the civilian structures of government in Srebrenica, and I can only speak of individuals that I attended -- where -- that I know. One of them is Osman Suljic and -- because we attended a meeting together. And I think that once or twice he also took part in meetings that were held at the UNPROFOR Potocari compound, under the auspices of the UNPROFOR commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions regarding this document, and I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As there is no translation yet, it will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 1D705 shall be assigned Exhibit D207. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now see D1805. Thank you. Can we pull it up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: I'm not sure if the accused said D or P185.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a VRS document signed by the commander, General Mladic, and it is one of the protest letters that he sent to the UNPROFOR commander personally at the time, General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the correct number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The correct number is D185. We have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General Mladic writes as follows, and I quote -- the document is dated 10 July 1995: "I received your letter from 9th of July, 1995. Srebrenica enclave has not been demilitarised in the spirit of the agreement of the 19th of April and 8th of May, 1993. Muslims did not surrender their weapons, mines, and explosives, and combat assets to UNPROFOR. Muslim forces are taking advantage of the special status of a protected zone for the preparation and execution of terrorist and other combat activities against the Serb people and the territory of Republika Srpska." Now, were you aware of the activities mentioned by General Mladic here, since they relate to the Srebrenica demilitarised zone, where you were at the time, and did you know that there were frequent requests and protests protesting the fact that the zone had not been and was not demilitarised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have information to that effect. I conveyed the requests sent by my superior commands and expressed our displeasure and frustration because of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Let me just read the second sentence now: "Allow me to remind you that from then up until now Muslim forces killed 100 and wounded over 200 Serb civilians in the attacks and with infiltrated sabotage-terrorist groups." Now, did you, too, point out the victims that were killed in the operations around the zone, the protected zone, and generally in the Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported all the victims and casualties in the area of responsibility of my brigade, whether they were military or civilian casualties, so that I had a list -- I had compiled a list, and I held it -- kept it within my brigade, a list of all those who had been killed from the moment that this area was proclaimed a demilitarised area up until almost the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, on the eve of the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We now see a document that you drafted and signed, a document coming from your brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next document: D185 was used by you with another witness, but at that point in time we didn't have a translation. There is a translation now. We see it on the screen. Are you tendering it now, finally?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we do wish to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will now be received.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we see a document -- or we will see a document that you sent to your superior command from your brigade. It is dated the 8th. Thank you. We will see it on our screens in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No document was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. 1D728. My apologies for not letting the e-court know. 1D728.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It has been registered, and I assume that on the 11th of July it was received by your command. That's what it says at the bottom. It was sent to the Drina Corps Command, the Intelligence Department, and also to General Krstic, the commander, personally, as well as to the forward command post. The first bullet point says: "In the enclave, there is total chaos and panic." The second bullet point: "The command chain has broken down. There is evidence of clashes between the existing command and Hakija Meholjic, who was appointed as the new commander pursuant to an order from the Main Staff of the BH army." And then it says: "Muslims are pulling out from Srebrenica and moving towards Potocari for Suceska." Now, can you tell us, according to this communication, this person was appointed as the new commander, and what information did you have about him when you drafted this report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is probably information that I had at the time that was reported to me. Now, whether Hakija Meholjic was, indeed, appointed as the new commander, I wasn't really sure then and I'm not even sure to this day, but I just conveyed and relayed the information that I had obtained and I felt that I needed to inform thereof my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information about the clashes between this person and the earlier leadership in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did have some information to the effect that Hakija Meholjic belonged to the second group - I call them factions, political factions - in Srebrenica and that he did not belong to the Naser Oric faction or the then commanders and the then politicians who were in charge of the civilian government. This was information that I had and that had to do with Hakija Meholjic. That's what I knew about him. Now, he was not the only one in his group -- they were not the only ones who were opponents of Naser Oric. There were other people too, such as Hamed Salihovic and other people who were in the enclave but were not -- did not see eye to eye with Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I ask this is that Meholjic, after the fall of the enclave, appeared in some public TV programmes, and perhaps you also had occasion to see this entire interview that was published in a newspaper, where he talked about the clashes within the enclave, how the enclave was actually traded off and in exchange for some territories, and so on. Did you hear of any of this? And I'm asking this because I will show you some more documents which also mention the clashes within the Muslim ranks and such as the one mentioned here in this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say this: I know that for a long time, there was general disorder in the enclave. There were all kinds of groups that were mutually opposed. On the one hand, we had Naser Oric and his group. Then there was Hakija Meholjic and his group. Then there was a third group, Ibrahim Mustafic and his group. And I believe that there was a fourth group headed by the former chief of the Public Security Station, Selimovic or Salihovic, Hamed. So these were the groups that were present in Srebrenica, and they were mutually opposed. What I know for a fact is that in Srebrenica enclave one could say that more or less everything was under the control of Naser Oric, whereas all the other groups were actually vying for their positions. And what I know is that between Srebrenica and Zepa, and Srebrenica and Tuzla, and Srebrenica and Kladanj, there were smuggling lines, and all sorts of goods were smuggled along those routes. So all these things were matters that I had information about and reported on regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned black-marketeering. We will discuss that a little later. I've already asked you about the internal strife and conflicts. Now I would like to show you P1174.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I'd like to stress that it's a sealed document, P1174, and it should not be shown in public. And in the meantime, could I also tender this document into evidence that we have on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1D728 will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 1D728 shall be assigned Exhibit D208, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we see this document that I called. Could we please show the second page of the document, once we've seen the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should do it in private session. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, can you help Mr. Tolimir and us with your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, since we were able to see from this statement that there were over 210 people killed on this road where the column was going from Srebrenica to Tuzla through Kamenica and Konjevic Polje and that there were stories about internal conflicts and erratic, odd behaviour, can you please tell us whether you had information about that and if you're able to tell us anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir. I can talk about what I knew, and that is that on that route along which the column was moving, from Srebrenica until it reached Tuzla, that there were quite a number of problems. As for specific features that are mentioned in this statement, that's data that I'm not familiar with. I wasn't there at the time, so I don't know what is accurate regarding the number of killed. Based on the information that I had at my disposal, I can say that there were mutual conflicts among some 15-, 16.000 people who had assembled and were supposed to set off for Tuzla. Also, based on information that I had later, after these events, indicates that there was shooting and mutual killing. What I do know for sure is that in front of the forward section of my brigade, in that area, there were many minefields that were laid, also individual mines, and that it's absolutely possible that as the column was moving, the people who were there could have encountered minefields and that they could have suffered mass casualties. Therefore, I can confirm that there were conflicts about how to organise the column, who was supposed to be at the head of the column, and so on. And this is information indicating that some people wanted to go to Zepa, some people wanted to go to Tuzla; there was disagreement about that. So this is two kinds of information that I have: that there were mutual conflicts, that also they had entered minefields; and that there were dead and wounded people there. Also, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I want to say that the column was constantly exposed to fire, that ambushes were organised in that sector by units that were present there, and that there were also people from the column killed due to that. This is what I can say, briefly, about what I knew at the time and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I would now like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, you are not continuing asking. We are already out of time again. We need our second break. And after that you may continue. We resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now you may put the question you wanted to ask before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, please, can we now look at another statement that we wanted to look at before. It's also something that should be shown in public -- in private session. We don't want to reveal the identity of the witness. We just want to deal with one sentence by this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at P -- Prosecutor 65 ter 1562. That's P1174. Or D151. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise, I made a mistake. I gave the wrong number to the Registry. We actually need D151, because I was actually looking for two different statements at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, paragraph 3, of this document. I will be very careful not to disclose anything about the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now look at line 4 -- actually, the last sentence in this line 4, which states: "From there, we headed towards Pobudjska Kamenica, where we met with a part of the first group, but the Chetniks surrounded us there and opened fire on us, killing over 300 people and wounding a large number. We were in disarray, as both soldiers and civilians started fleeing wherever they could, while the wounded were left behind on the path." Please, I don't want to quote anything else from this statement. I just want to ask you this. This is the same incident that the previous witness spoke about, where this witness said he saw 300 victims and the previous one said he saw 150. So these are the numbers given on the road as the column was moving towards Pobudjska Kamenica. My question is: As you were receiving information, and you said earlier that there were losses, that there were significant casualties due to artillery fire at the Muslim column that was moving towards Pobudjska Kamenica, and did you hear later that there were also victims there when everything was over? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew in my brigade, at that point in time when the column was moving, is that the column was having problems. I already explained what these problems were relating to the conflicts and other things. I also said that I had information about how there were constant problems on the route that the column was taking, there were ambushes and fighting from the Serb forces, and that on that route there was a large number of people who were hurt, killed, wounded. This is what I knew, in general. I just want to note here that these individual cases of this nature that you are presenting to me from these statements are something that I am not familiar with. I did, perhaps, see from statements that mass killings are mentioned or that people died en masse, that they came into minefields, and so on. So these details were something that I did not have at that point in time as the column was moving along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These statements are by Prosecution witnesses who survived the incident. They all talk about a large number of casualties. Do you know if that large number of casualties is something -- actually, those bodies, were they picked up during "asanacija," and is that where information about a large number of casualties subsequently came from? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone going from that area along that route and picking up the bodies and burying them. I'm not ruling out the possibility that somebody did do that. But knowing that area and where the column was moving, I doubt if anybody was going there in an organised manner and picking up the dead bodies from places in that area. I know something else for a fact that is relating to the presence of a lady. I'm not going to reveal her name. She's from Finland. She came after the operation, asking to be taken along the route in order to check stories that there were still clothes and skeletons strewn about that area. I think - I repeat, I think - that a large number of people who were killed along that route were not picked up and not buried. I'm talking about the state of affairs after the operation was carried out. Later, activities were undertaken in order to find and look for all of those mass places, and the skeletons or the bodily remains of those people who were killed were collected. And as far as I know, subsequently they were collected and buried in a common grave in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just mentioned the Finnish pathologist, as Mr. Jean-Rene mentioned during the identification in the Bare Sector. He said there were 600 of them. And then later it was said that they were taken to Tuzla. It says here that they were taken to Tuzla. Do you know what the Finnish team was doing there in that area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for a fact is that the lady insisted that she goes to that sector. The Serbian side was not inclined for her to go along that entire route which she insisted on. The main reason for that was because representatives of the Serbian side knew that there was a large number of minefields and individual mines that were left behind. They proposed to her certain sections. So it wasn't a matter of whether she would be taken there or not. It was simply of taking her to places that were passable and where she could see what she wanted to see safely. I don't know anything else about their work, except for being present one day in that area of responsibility of my unit one day. I think they did go and tour one sector there, but I'm not familiar with the particulars because that was not something that I was involved in. I think she was escorted by the civilian police, or I don't know who, but I was not part of those activities, so I don't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that this Finnish lady was Helena Ranta; do you maybe remember the name? Does that name tell you anything, Helena Ranta? That's the person mentioned by the demographers and by the Investigator Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Really, I don't know. I wouldn't like to speculate. I only know that she was from Finland.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. They said that she found 600 persons at that location, Bare. Jean-Rene Ruez said it. Then we also saw another number, 500. So that's already 1.000. Do you know that all those persons are accounted as if they were shot and killed at the same place, and now people are charged with their deaths, although they are people who were killed in combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may put questions to the witness, but it's not for you to make a statement about numbers. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, with respect to the numbers, I understand, from the general's questions, that he's saying that J.R. Ruez talked about 600 persons. Then he threw out another number, 500. And I'd like to know what the basis of that statement regarding another 500 bodies is, especially if he's going to add them together and claim that they're all from the same area, especially if he's going to make the further claims that Your Honour just pointed out at the end of the question. I'd just like to know what the factual basis is for this question before it's put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us with the basis of your information?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The basis is the statement given by Jean-Rene Ruez. He testified here. I already quoted the statement on a number of occasions. And if it is necessary, I can quote it again to this witness. But I think it isn't necessary. The second basis is the statement P174, relating to the Pobudjska Kamenica site. And also the basis is the witness statement mentioned 300 dead near Pobudjska Kamenica. That's the basis to add 600 and 300 and the 40 that I mentioned at the beginning and that 30 that I mentioned earlier. Thank you. I'm referring to 1174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And can you give us a reference to the testimony of Witness Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will give you the reference. 1D100, page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to make sure that the record is clear. My question had to do with this figure of 500. Are we to understand that this figure of 500 is based upon adding together various totals or estimates that have been provided by a number of different witnesses and so he's lumping them into one number, 500; or is he saying that there's one witness somewhere that talked about 500 and that that figure of 500 was located in the same area as his figure for 600 ? That's all we're asking. He's thrown out a bunch of numbers, 30, 300, 40, and if it's his case that he's adding up various witness statements who talk about 40 here, 30 there, and 300, then, okay, but we want to know where he gets this allegation that there is another 500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you said that you have taken the number from the testimony of Mr. Ruez. Now you have a reference to a document we haven't seen yet, 1D100. This is not the transcript in this case. I think you should rephrase your question. That makes it easier to follow. And ask the witness without putting all these numbers to the witness. Otherwise, we really need some more references. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In answer to your question, at page 72, lines 4 to 8, just now you've stated: "Later, activities were undertaken in order to find and look for all of those mass places, and the skeletons or the bodily remains of those people who were killed were collected. And as far as I know, subsequently they were collected and buried in a common grave in Potocari." Who collected and buried these people in this common grave in Potocari; do you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that subsequently other locations were found and people were collected there and buried, I was referring to the period after this operation and after all these activities. I was referring to a longer period of time after that, because it took a long time to find all those people on that path, and I think that this hasn't finished. I think that the search is still going on to find the people who were killed or who lost their lives. That's what I meant when I said that they were found later. As far as I know, I'm not aware of any other location, except for individual cases. So I don't know for any other case that people who were in the column lost their lives and were buried at any other place other than Potocari. That's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Please wait. I have a follow-up question for the witness. I would like to come back to the last question of Mr. Tolimir. I see the essence of his question was, in fact, Do you know the total number of dead people in the column and in the field where the column was moving to the north; do you know the total number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never testified that I know the total number. Even now I don't know it. That's something that I never was interested in. In my testimony so far and in my statements in general, I mentioned estimates based on everything that I saw and based on everything that I knew about the enclave and what was going on there, so they were only estimates. Now, what is the actual number of people killed and people buried, I really don't know that. I never went into it, except, as a normal human being, I'm following what is going on in relation to this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another question. Do you have any knowledge about the percentage of people, of those who were killed in the column, who were killed in combat? A percentage in relation to those who were not killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the preparation for my defence, I read every statement and I knew the numbers because this was the basis which enabled me to either affirm or deny things that were within my knowledge. So I can give an estimate, but you shouldn't take it as something that I know as a fact. Based on everything that I know, the ratio of people who were executed and people who were killed in various other ways, in combat activities, in ambushes, by shelling, in other fighting, is maybe 92 or 93 per cent people who were executed and, according to my estimates, 7, 8, maybe up to 10 per cent of people who maybe lost their lives on the path between Srebrenica and Tuzla. It's a rough estimate. I'm not sure about it. I don't know the actual numbers, but this is my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I'm only interested in the people who were in the column moving to the north. Many of them lost their lives on their way to the north. How many per cent of them were, in effect, killed in combat? Have you any idea about that, or even knowledge? I'm only referring to the column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I know, and I can only tell you what I know, and according to my estimate and the estimate of everybody who looked into the matter, there were between 15-, and 16.000 people in that column. This column split up at a certain point, and that part which managed to break through to Tuzla numbered between 4-, and 5.000 people. I'm speaking on the basis of the information that I have. Another part went towards Zepa. Another part was captured and transferred to Bratunac later on. My estimate is that between 3-, and 4.000 people from the column lost their lives, but I don't know. I really don't know. I think it makes no sense for me to go on speculating. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to speculate. Only I was asking for your knowledge from different sources. Do you have any knowledge about the percentage, among those who lost their lives in the column, how many of them were combatants and killed in combat? If you don't know, if you only can speculate, that's fine. But if you have knowledge, I would be interested in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't want to speculate. I don't have that knowledge. I was never really dealing with this subject-matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just now, at page 77, lines 11 to 17, you have stated that: "Based on everything that I know, the ratio of people who were executed and people who were killed in various other ways, in combat activities, in ambushes, by shelling, in other fighting, is maybe 92 or 93 per cent people who were executed and, according to my estimates, 7, 8, and maybe 10 per cent of people who lost their lives on the path between Srebrenica and Tuzla." How do you come to this estimate? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis for this estimate is my knowledge about the number of people who were separated in Potocari. Also, and I'm now talking here about an estimate, I saw the number of people who were captured during this whole period at that spot and on the path from Srebrenica to Konjevic Polje and further on. So I base my estimate on those data, counting all the people who were separated in Potocari, those who were captured and temporarily detained in Bratunac and Kravica. So if we take all this into account, then my estimate is that around 10 per cent of all Srebrenica-related victims lost their lives in combat. The rest was detained and later executed. Whether it was in Bratunac or in Zvornik, I don't know. I'm simply talking about the general number. And, of course, I'm giving you my estimates. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, while we still have this document on the screen, the document talking about the Bare location, take a look at line 8, which says: "This area has been processed in 1996 by a team of experts from Finland who were operating in that area in 1996, totally disconnected from our activities. They were collecting surface remains. But it's important to note that 600 bodies have been collected in that area." So he's referring here to Bare: "These are bodies of victims killed in combat, in ambushes, in shelling, and possibly also in other circumstances which are impossible to sort out between -- I mean, for us, at least, between combat and other situations." End quote, line 17. My question is: Do you know the distance between Bare and Pobudjska Kamenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact distance. Without a map, I wouldn't be able to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the same location or is there some distance between Pobudjska Kamenica, that this witness refers to, and Bare, that Mr. Ruez refers to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's some distance between them, but I wouldn't like to speculate. I don't know exactly where Bare is. I heard of Bare, but I don't know where that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, for the sake of the record, you were reading from the transcript in the Krstic case, where the Witness Ruez testified, and this is 1D100. And in our case, it's now D166. And to understand your last question, you said: Is it the same location or is it some distance between ... Kamenica, that this witness refers to ..." Which witness do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was thinking of Witness Ruez, on one page, and Witness -- protected witness who speaks about this in their statement that we looked at a little bit earlier here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. This is sufficient. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in view of numerous statements talking about a certain number of killed -- we're not going to refer to a number, we don't want an objection by the Trial Chamber, but we would like to at some point have a specific figure so that at least we know. But what my question is: This number, 600 people from the Bare location and that 300-odd number that encountered minefields and other things, as we read in the witness's statement, all of those bodies, were they brought into a common grave, and were they all presented as victims who were killed by Serbs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer this question on the basis of what I know. I've been in prison for 10 years now, so there are a lot of things that have changed that relate to the burials since I have been serving my sentence in prison. What I know is that all the victims who happened to be in the column and had lost their lives in any of a different manner were probably buried in Potocari, which applies to all of those who were killed in 1995, those who were killed individually or who were killed in different ways. They were buried in the Potocari grave. I think that there were individual cases when somebody did not want them to be buried there. This is something that I was following in the press, and this is something that I know -- that I've read about during the time-period that I've been in jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The total number of victims, has it been presented to all the accused as some kind of responsibility or charge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes, that the victims and the number of victims is something that is among those things that the accused are being charged with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at D64. That's a document that I signed, and we will only quote relevant portions of it about the separation, or, rather, the registering of all those who are able-bodied. I am reading from the document: "On 12th of July of this year, at 1945 hours, a radio network of elements of the 28th Muslim Division was activated. During the morning, at around 0500 hours, these elements came across our minefield in the sector of Ravni Buljin at the juncture between the Milici and Bratunac Brigades." And then it goes on to say -- can you look at the third paragraph from the bottom, and can we look at the first dash, where they're talking about the direction through which parts of the broken 28th Muslim Division are going to pull out from Srebrenica. They are to take all measures to prevent pull-out and capture the enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: This document which was sent to you -- actually, it wasn't sent to you. It was sent to the Intelligence Sector of the Drina Corps from the Sarajevo and Eastern Bosnian Corps. Does this document not say that the Main Staff suggests that you propose to the commanders such and such a thing; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the way it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll up. Can we look at the last line at the bottom, where it says that: "The Muslims wish to portray Srebrenica as a demilitarised zone, with nothing but a civilian population in it. That is why they ordered all armed men fit for military service to illegally pull out from the area across RS territory and reach the Muslim-controlled area so that they could accuse the VRS of an unprovoked attack on civilians in a safe haven." And then it further states: "Although it is very important to arrest as many members of the shattered Muslim units as possible, or liquidate them if they resist, it is equally important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question is this: Since you are being asked to propose to the commanders to register and evacuate, can you be responsible for that, and can your commanders be held responsible for that because they ordered you to do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, General, sir, if I understood your question entirely. But if you're asking me if my commander is responsible for something that is happening in his unit's AOR, I'm going to tell you, yes, my commander is responsible for that. If you are asking me whether I feel responsible for the activities that I was ordered to execute or are part of my remit, then I must say that I do feel responsible for all the assignments that were entrusted to me and that I was executing, if that's what you were asking. I'm not sure that I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is 7.00. We have to adjourn for the day. I would like to mention an omission at the beginning of today's hearing. I didn't welcome Ms. Lindsay to this hearing as well, and I would like to state on the record that you have been with us the whole session of today. We have to adjourn for today, but Mr. Thayer wants to raise a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could get an estimate as to how much cross-examination is required further from the Defence. We have another witness who's ready, and it would be helpful to know when to have that witness available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, we're going to use all the time that we have said we would use and all the time that you have accorded to us based on the extensions that Mr. Thayer used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecution used nine and a half hours, and Mr. Tolimir, up to now, six hours and forty-two minutes. It is quite unlikely that we will conclude with this witness's testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn. I have to remind you, you have to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom, and it is not allowed to have contact about the content of your testimony to either party. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
